{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"A device is not fully owned when its maker can disable features after sale. Ownership is supposed to transfer control, not merely possession of a shell. If the seller retains a switch that can remove an advertised function (its software, service access, or compatibility), the transaction leaves a continuing hierarchy inside the product. The buyer holds the object; the maker still governs part of what it can do—and can govern it after the money has changed hands.

That distinction matters because modern devices are layered products. Hardware depends on firmware, accounts, authentication servers, and permissions. A feature may be physically present yet unavailable because code refuses to activate it. Digital restrictions management (DRM) makes this familiar in media, but the ownership problem reaches appliances, vehicles, medical equipment, and tools. The lock isn't less consequential because it is written in software.

Manufacturers may have legitimate reasons to maintain remote controls. A dangerous defect could require prompt intervention, and network services need defenses against abuse. Yet those purposes do not justify an unlimited power to subtract capabilities from purchased goods. A narrowly tailored safety response is one thing; a permanent authority to revise the bargain is another. When the same channel can protect a device or diminish it (including its sensors and local functions), incentives matter.

Consider the practical test: after the warranty ends, who decides whether the feature keeps working? If the answer is always the maker, the buyer doesn't possess final authority. The arrangement resembles a house sale in which the former owner keeps the key to one room (a camera, battery mode, or diagnostic interface) and reserves the right to lock it later. Calling that room “software” can't make the retained key disappear.

This power also changes competition. A maker that can deactivate compatibility can steer owners toward approved accessories, subscriptions, or repair channels. Even when the immediate reason sounds benign (security or quality control), the architecture permits commercial pressure—power that follows the product through resale. Secondary buyers inherit terms they never negotiated, while independent technicians may find working hardware blocked by an authorization check.

Consumer law should recognize remote disablement for what it is: continuing control after payment. Sellers should disclose every feature that depends on external authorization (not merely internet connectivity), state how long support will last, and provide a durable local mode when that support ends. They should not be allowed to market a capability as part of a sale while reserving an undisclosed right to erase it later.

Repair rules need the same clarity. Access to parts and manuals won't establish meaningful ownership if software can still reject a lawful replacement. Owners and independent services (repair shops, refurbishers, and recyclers) need tools to restore purchased functions without seeking perpetual permission. A security exception may be necessary, but it should be specific, reviewable, and no broader than the demonstrated risk—not a blank check labeled “safety.”

As digital-rights advocates, we should press lawmakers and regulators to treat post-sale feature removal as a core ownership issue. Require clear disclosure, meaningful consent for material changes, restoration where feasible, and refunds when promised functions vanish. Ask the concrete question before accepting any ownership claim: can you keep using the purchased feature if the maker (the maker, not the current owner) changes its mind? A device is not fully owned when its maker can disable features after sale. Ownership is supposed to transfer control, not merely possession of a shell. If the seller retains a switch that can remove an advertised function (its software, service access, or compatibility), the transaction leaves a continuing hierarchy inside the product. The buyer holds the object; the maker still governs part of what it can do—and can govern it after the money has changed hands.

That distinction matters because modern devices are layered products. Hardware depends on firmware, accounts, authentication servers, and permissions. A feature may be physically present yet unavailable because code refuses to activate it. Digital restrictions management (DRM) makes this familiar in media, but the ownership problem reaches appliances, vehicles, medical equipment, and tools. The lock isn't less consequential because it is written in software.

Manufacturers may have legitimate reasons to maintain remote controls. A dangerous defect could require prompt intervention, and network services need defenses against abuse. Yet those purposes do not justify an unlimited power to subtract capabilities from purchased goods. A narrowly tailored safety response is one thing; a permanent authority to revise the bargain is another. When the same channel can protect a device or diminish it (including its sensors and local functions), incentives matter.

Consider the practical test: after the warranty ends, who decides whether the feature keeps working? If the answer is always the maker, the buyer doesn't possess final authority. The arrangement resembles a house sale in which the former owner keeps the key to one room (a camera, battery mode, or diagnostic interface) and reserves the right to lock it later. Calling that room “software” can't make the retained key disappear.

This power also changes competition. A maker that can deactivate compatibility can steer owners toward approved accessories, subscriptions, or repair channels. Even when the immediate reason sounds benign (security or quality control), the architecture permits commercial pressure—power that follows the product through resale. Secondary buyers inherit terms they never negotiated, while independent technicians may find working hardware blocked by an authorization check.

Consumer law should recognize remote disablement for what it is: continuing control after payment. Sellers should disclose every feature that depends on external authorization (not merely internet connectivity), state how long support will last, and provide a durable local mode when that support ends. They should not be allowed to market a capability as part of a sale while reserving an undisclosed right to erase it later.

Repair rules need the same clarity. Access to parts and manuals won't establish meaningful ownership if software can still reject a lawful replacement. Owners and independent services (repair shops, refurbishers, and recyclers) need tools to restore purchased functions without seeking perpetual permission. A security exception may be necessary, but it should be specific, reviewable, and no broader than the demonstrated risk—not a blank check labeled “safety.”

As digital-rights advocates, we should press lawmakers and regulators to treat post-sale feature removal as a core ownership issue. Require clear disclosure, meaningful consent for material changes, restoration where feasible, and refunds when promised functions vanish. Ask the concrete question before accepting any ownership claim: can you keep using the purchased feature if the maker (the maker, not the current owner) changes its mind? If the answer is no, that's a license wearing the costume of a sale—and our law should say so.
